llm_summary: The run built a powerful offensive deck and defeated the Act 1 boss, but Act 2 steadily converted a healthy start into severe HP attrition. The decisive failure was defensive prioritization in the Collector fight: while already at 22 HP and facing an attack, the agent chose damage over a legal Iron Wave, then entered later turns with almost no margin for error. The earlier choice to recall for the Ruby Key instead of resting also left little recovery opportunity during the subsequent sequence of Act 2 combats.

llm_lessons.title: At low HP, prefer survival over nonlethal damage
llm_lessons.situation: When HP is low, the enemy is attacking, and a block-producing card is legally playable but the enemy is not close to dying.
llm_lessons.lesson: Treat defensive attacks such as Iron Wave as higher priority than pure damage when survival is uncertain. In the Collector fight, at 22 HP with Collector at 155 HP, Iron Wave was available for 4 energy, but Bludgeon+ and then Headbutt were chosen; preserve a damage buffer unless the available attack sequence is demonstrably lethal.
evidence_points: Turn 11: at 22/74 HP with Collector at 155 HP, Iron Wave was a legal alternative alongside Bludgeon+, but Bludgeon+ was chosen.
Turn 11 afterward: with 1 energy and Collector at 113 HP, Headbutt was chosen while Iron Wave was still a legal alternative in the hand.
The next logged state was still 22/74 HP with Collector attacking, followed by later turns reaching 2/74 HP.
llm_lessons.reasoning: The enemy was far from dead, so the offensive sequence did not establish a lethal race. Choosing the available block option would at least have preserved some protection before the attack, whereas the chosen attacks left the run dependent on drawing immediate defense.

llm_lessons.title: Do not spend a healthy campfire on a key without a recovery plan
llm_lessons.situation: At an Act 2 campfire, when HP is healthy but the remaining route has already shown repeated combat damage and the key can potentially be obtained at another opportunity.
llm_lessons.lesson: Before taking a required key at a campfire, compare it against resting: if the upcoming Act 2 sequence is likely to contain several fights and there is no later confirmed rest, preserve HP unless the key timing is essential.
evidence_points: At Act 2 floor 23, HP was 71/74 and the campfire alternatives were rest or recall; recall for the Ruby Key was chosen.
After that point, HP reached 49/74 at floor 24, then recovered to 74/74, but fell through 57/74, 45/74, 35/74, and 32/74 across later Act 2 combat rewards.
No later REST_DECISION appears before the Collector fight, where the run eventually reached 2/74 HP.
llm_lessons.reasoning: The recall obtained a necessary key, but it also consumed the only explicitly logged recovery opportunity before a long chain of Act 2 combats. The lesson is not to abandon keys, but to plan key timing around available healing rather than spending a healthy campfire automatically.

llm_lessons.title: Use block before entering a repeated attack cycle
llm_lessons.situation: When an enemy is attacking and the current hand has no guaranteed kill, especially after already losing a large amount of HP in the fight.
llm_lessons.lesson: Do not defer defense merely because the enemy is progressing toward a low HP total. In the Collector fight, once HP was 22 or lower, sequence attacks around available block and avoid ending turns with zero block unless the kill is secured.
evidence_points: Turn 12 began at 22/74 HP with Collector at 104 HP and attacking; the hand contained Immolate, Cleave, and Headbutt but no block card, after the previous turn had used attacks instead of the legal Iron Wave.
Turn 13 began at 2/74 HP with Collector at 81 HP and attacking; Iron Wave was legal, but Bash+ was played first, followed by Iron Wave only after spending energy.
The final combat ended with the player at 2/74 HP while Collector still had 64 HP in the last logged state.
llm_lessons.reasoning: The fight had not reached a lethal threshold, so maximizing damage while repeatedly leaving the player exposed created an unsustainable HP race. Defense needed to be planned one turn earlier, when the player still had enough HP to survive an imperfect draw.
